sourceDesc.p: The text of this edition is the Perseus Project's double-keyboarded transcription (c. 2003) of The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, ed. William George Clark and William Aldis Wright (Garden City, New York: Nelson Doubleday, Inc.), 2 vols. (OCLC 08687211; Tufts University's Tisch Library holds two catalog records for this set, both giving the date only as "19--"). All's Well That Ends Well is in volume 2, consulted in the Internet Archive copy bwb_S0-ATQ-198 (pp. 635-662); its date of printing is not confirmed. That edition reprints the Globe text in a setting of its own, with American spellings, which the transcription keeps. In some readings the transcription departs from both the copy-text and the Globe; the cause has not been established.

The Globe line numbering is not taken from the copy-text. It is read from two page-image witnesses to the Globe itself, printed from the same plates two decades apart: The Works of William Shakespeare, Cambridge and London: Macmillan, 1866 (HathiTrust miun.aba6868.0001.001, University of Michigan copy, catalog record 000241315) and The Works of William Shakespeare, London: Macmillan, 1887 (Internet Archive worksofwilliamsh0000shak_y3h8, Trent University copy, OCLC 1158473505).

editorialDecl.p: Words and structure -- divisions, speakers, speeches, stage directions, and verse lines where the copy-text sets verse -- are the double-keyboarded text, unaltered. Where a witness page disagrees with it over a word, the transcription stands and the disagreement is recorded in the project's reports.

The Globe lineation was regenerated from the witnesses in 2026. Each printed row of the witness page was classified by its typography, Globe lines were assembled from those rows, and the resulting count was checked on every page against every line number printed in that page's margins; a page whose count disagreed with any printed number was not accepted. In ten places in this play the page's typography does not show where a Globe line begins: two speeches that may share a verse line, a speech's line continued on a row set flush with the margin, or a row set as though it completed the line above which the Globe numbers as a line of its own. These were decided individually, from the page images and the printed line numbers and, where the page is silent, from the line division of the Folger edition, All's Well That Ends Well, ed. Barbara A. Mowat and Paul Werstine, Folger Digital Texts, version 0.5 (Washington, DC: Folger Shakespeare Library, 2015), as distributed in the Shakespeare Drama Corpus (ShakeDraCor, play shake000012; github.com/dracor-org/shakedracor, commit c34c2d4). The Folger was consulted only for its division of shared lines, never for words or numbers. Each decision is recorded in the project's data tables.

The Globe line numbers previously carried by the Perseus edition were transcribed from the copy-text and are not retained. They are consistent with the numbering below, but were placed by a different convention.
First Folio through-line numbers are not carried by this edition. They remain in the Perseus P4 edition.

encodingDesc.p: <milestone unit="line" ed="Globe"> marks the first word of a Globe line, and every Globe line carries one, numbered. A Globe line may occupy more than one printed row: a verse line too long for the column, or a line shared between two speakers. <lb/> marks each printed row that begins no Globe line. A Globe milestone therefore also marks the start of a printed row, and reconstructing the page's rows requires reading both elements.

The @part attribute, which marks the parts of a verse line shared between speakers, is retained from the Perseus P4 edition and was not regenerated. It does not always agree with the Globe's division of shared lines; where the two differ, the Globe milestones govern the numbering.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter BERTRAM, the COUNTESS OF ROUSILLON,
HELENA, and LAFEU, all in black.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: In delivering my son from me, I bury a second husband.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And I in going, madam, weep o'er my father's death anew: but I must attend his majesty's command, to whom I am now in ward, evermore in subjection.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You shall find of the king a husband, madam; you, sir, a father: he that so generally is at all times good must of necessity hold his virtue to you; whose worthiness would stir it up where it wanted rather than lack it where there is such abundance.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: What hope is there of his majesty's amendment?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: He hath abandoned his physicians, madam; under whose practices he hath persecuted time with hope, and finds no other advantage in the process but only the losing of hope by time.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: This young gentlewoman had a father,--O that 'had'! how sad a passage 'tis!-- whose skill was almost as great as his honesty; had it stretched so far, would have made nature immortal, and death should have play for lack of work. Would, for the king's sake, he were living! I think it would be the death of the king's disease.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: How called you the man you speak of, madam?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: He was famous, sir, in his profession, and it was his great right to be so: Gerard de Narbon.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: He was excellent indeed, madam: the king very lately spoke of him admiringly and mourningly: he was skilful enough to have lived still, if knowledge could be set up against mortality.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What is it, my good lord, the king languishes of?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: A fistula, my lord.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I heard not of it before.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I would it were not notorious. Was this gentlewoman the daughter of Gerard de Narbon?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: His sole child, my lord, and bequeathed to my overlooking. I have those hopes of her good that her education promises; her dispositions she inherits, which makes fair gifts fairer; for where an unclean mind carries virtuous qualities, there commendations go with pity; they are virtues and traitors too; in her they are the better for their simpleness; she derives her honesty and achieves her goodness.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Your commendations, madam, get from her tears.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: 'Tis the best brine a maiden can season her praise in. The remembrance of her father never approaches her heart but the tyranny of her sorrows takes all livelihood from her cheek. No more of this, Helena; go to, no more; lest it be rather thought you affect a sorrow than have it.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I do affect a sorrow indeed, but I have it too.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Moderate lamentation is the right of the dead, excessive grief the enemy to the living.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: If the living be enemy to the grief, the excess makes it soon mortal.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Madam, I desire your holy wishes.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: How understand we that?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Be thou blest, Bertram, and succeed
thy father in manners, as in shape! thy blood and virtue Contend for empire in thee, and thy goodness Share with thy birthright! Love all, trust a few, Do wrong to none: be able for thine enemy Rather in power than use, and keep thy friend Under thy own life's key; be check'd for silence, But never tax'd for speech. What heaven more
will, That thee may furnish and my prayers pluck
down, Fall on thy head! Farewell, my lord; 'Tis an unseason'd courtier; good my lord, Advise him.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: He cannot want the best That shall attend his love.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Heavens bless him! Farewell, Bertram.
[Exit.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: The best wishes that can be forged in your thoughts be servants to you! Be comfortable to my mother, your mistress, and make much of her.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
Farewell, pretty lady: you must hold the credit of your father.
[Exeunt Bertram and Lafeu.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
O, were that all! I think not on my
father; And these great tears grace his remembrance
more Than those I shed for him. What was he like? I have forgot him: my imagination Carries no favour in't but Bertram's. I am undone: there is no living, none, If Bertram be away. 'Twere all one That I should love a bright particular star And think to wed it, he is so above me: In his bright radiance and collateral light Must I be comforted, not in his sphere. The ambition in my love thus plagues itself: The hind that would be mated by the lion Must die for love. 'Twas pretty, though a plague, To see him every hour; to sit and draw His arched brows, his hawking eye, his curls, In our heart's table; heart too capable Of every line and trick of his sweet favour: But now he's gone, and my idolatrous fancy Must sanctify his reliques. Who comes here?
Enter PAROLLES.
[Aside] One that goes with him: I love him for
his sake; And yet I know him a notorious liar, Think him a great way fool, solely a coward; Yet these fix'd evils sit so fit in him, That they take place, when virtue's steely bones Look bleak i' the cold wind: withal, full oft we see Cold wisdom waiting on superfluous folly.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Save you, fair queen!

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: And you, monarch!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: And no.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Are you meditating on virginity?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Ay. You have some stain of soldier in you: let me ask you a question. Man is enemy to virginity; how may we barricado it against him?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Keep him out.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: But he assails; and our virginity, though valiant, in the defence yet is weak: unfold to us some warlike resistance.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: There is none: man, sitting down before you, will undermine you and blow you up.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Bless our poor virginity from underminers and blowers up! Is there no military policy, how virgins might blow up men?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Virginity being blown down, man will quicklier be blown up: marry, in blowing him down again, with the breach yourselves made, you lose your city. It is not politic in the commonwealth of nature to preserve virginity. Loss of virginity is rational increase and there was never virgin got till virginity was first lost. That you were made of is metal to make virgins. Virginity by being once lost may be ten times found; by being ever kept, it is ever lost: 'tis too cold a companion; away with 't!

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I will stand for't a little, though therefore I die a virgin.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: There's little can be said in't; 'tis against the rule of nature. To speak on the part of virginity, is to accuse your mothers; which is most infallible disobedience. He that hangs himself is a virgin; virginity murders itself and should be buried in highways out of all sanctified limit, as a desperate offendress against nature. Virginity breeds mites, much like a cheese; consumes itself to the very paring, and so dies with feeding his own stomach. Besides, virginity is peevish, proud, idle, made of self-love, which is the most inhibited sin in the canon. Keep it not; you cannot choose but lose by 't: out with't! within ten year it will make itself ten, which is a goodly increase; and the principal itself not much the worse: away with 't!

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: How might one do, sir, to lose it to her own liking?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Let me see: marry, ill, to like him that ne'er it likes. 'Tis a commodity will lose the gloss with lying; the longer kept, the less worth: off with't while 'tis vendible; answer the time of request. Virginity, like an old courtier, wears her cap out of fashion: richly suited, but unsuitable: just like the brooch and the tooth-pick, which wear not now. Your date is better in your pie and your porridge than in your cheek: and your virginity, your old virginity is like one of our French withered pears, it looks ill, it eats drily; marry, 'tis a withered pear; it was formerly better; marry, yet 'tis a withered pear: will you anything with it?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Not my virginity yet. . . . There shall your master have a thousand loves, A mother and a mistress and a friend, A phoenix, captain and an enemy, A guide, a goddess, and a sovereign, A counsellor, a traitress, and a dear; His humble ambition, proud humility, His jarring concord, and his discord dulcet, His faith, his sweet disaster; with a world Of pretty, fond, adoptious christendoms, That blinking Cupid gossips. Now shall he-- I know not what he shall. God send him well! The court's a learning place, and he is one--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What one, i' faith?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: That I wish well. 'Tis pity--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What's pity?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
That wishing well had not a body in 't, Which might be felt; that we, the poorer born, Whose baser stars do shut us up in wishes, Might with effects of them follow our friends, And show what we alone must think, which never Return us thanks.
Enter Page.

sp.speaker: Page.
sp.p: Monsieur Parolles, my lord calls for you. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Little Helen, farewell; if I can remember thee, I will think of thee at court.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Monsieur Parolles, you were born under a charitable star.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Under Mars, I.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I especially think, under Mars.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why under Mars?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: The wars have so kept you under that you must needs be born under Mars.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: When he was predominant.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: When he was retrograde, I think, rather.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why think you so?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: You go so much backward when you fight.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: That's for advantage.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: So is running away, when fear proposes the safety: but the composition that your valour and fear makes in you is a virtue of a good wing, and I like the wear well.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I am so full of businesses, I cannot answer thee acutely. I will return perfect courtier; in the which, my instruction shall serve to naturalize thee, so thou wilt be capable of a courtier's counsel and understand what advice shall thrust upon thee; else thou diest in thine unthankfulness, and thine ignorance makes thee away: farewell. When thou hast leisure, say thy prayers; when thou hast none, remember thy friends: get thee a good husband, and use him as he uses thee; so farewell. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Our remedies oft in ourselves do lie. Which we ascribe to heaven: the fated sky Gives us free scope, only doth backward pull Our slow designs when we ourselves are dull. What power is it which mounts my love so high, That makes me see, and cannot feed mine eye? The mightiest space in fortune nature brings To join like likes and kiss like native things. Impossible be strange attempts to those That weigh their pains in sense and do suppose What hath been cannot be: who ever strove To show her merit, that did miss her love? The king's disease--my project may deceive me, But my intents are fix'd and will not leave me. [Exit.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage:
Enter the KING OF FRANCE,
with letters, and divers Attendants.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
The Florentines and Senoys are by the
ears; Have fought with equal fortune and continue
A braving war.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: So 'tis reported, sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Nay, 'tis most credible; we here
receive it A certainty, vouch'd from our cousin Austria, With caution that the Florentine will move us For speedy aid; wherein our dearest friend Prejudicates the business and would seem To have us make denial.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: His love and wisdom, Approved so to your majesty, may plead For amplest credence.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: He hath arm'd our answer, And Florence is denied before he comes: Yet, for our gentlemen that mean to see The Tuscan service, freely have they leave To stand on either part.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p: It well may serve A nursery to our gentry, who are sick For breathing and exploit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
What's he comes here?
Enter BERTRAM, LAFEU, and PAROLLES.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p:
It is the Count Rousillon, my
good lord, Young Bertram.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Youth, thou bear'st thy father's face; Frank nature, rather curious than in haste, Hath well composed thee. Thy father's moral
parts Mayst thou inherit too! Welcome to Paris.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: My thanks and duty are your majesty's.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
I would I had that corporal soundness
now, As when thy father and myself in friendship First tried our soldiership! He did look far Into the service of the time and was Discipled of the bravest: he lasted long; But on us both did haggish age steal on And wore us out of act. It much repairs me To talk of your good father. In his youth He had the wit which I can well observe To-day in our young lords; but they may jest Till their own scorn return to them unnoted Ere they can hide their levity in honor: So like a courtier, contempt nor bitterness Were in his pride or sharpness; if they were, His equal had awaked them, and his honour, Clock to itself, knew the true minute when Exception bid him speak, and at this time His tongue obey'd his hand: who were below him He used as creatures of another place And bow'd his eminent top to their low ranks, Making them proud of his humility, In their poor praise he humbled. Such a man Might be a copy to these younger times; Which, follow'd well, would demonstrate them now But goers backward.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: His good remembrance, sir, Lies richer in your thoughts than on his tomb; So in approof lives not his epitaph As in your royal speech.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Would I were with him! He would
always say-- Methinks I hear him now; his plausive words He scatter'd not in ears, but grafted them, To grow there and to bear,--'Let me not live,'-- This his good melancholy oft began, On the catastrophe and heel of pastime, When it was out,--'Let me not live,' quoth he, 'After my flame lacks oil, to be the snuff Of younger spirits, whose apprehensive senses All but new things disdain; whose judgements
are Mere fathers of their garments; whose constancies Expire before their fashions.' This he wish'd: I after him do after him wish too, Since I nor wax nor honey can bring home, I quickly were dissolved from my hive, To give some labourers room.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p: You are loved, sir: They that least lend it you shall lack you first.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
I fill a place, I know't. How long is't,
count, Since the physician at your father's died? He was much famed.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Some six months since, my lord.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: If he were living, I would try him yet. Lend me an arm; the rest have worn me out With several applications: nature and sickness Debate it at their leisure. Welcome, count; My son's no dearer.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
Thank your majesty.
[Exeunt. Flourish.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I will now hear; what say you of this gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Madam, the care I have had to even your content, I wish might be found in the calendar of my past endeavours; for then we wound our modesty and make foul the clearness of our deservings, when of ourselves we publish them.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: What does this knave here? Get you gone, sirrah: the complaints I have heard of you I do not all believe; 'tis my slowness that I do not; for I know you lack not folly to commit them, and have ability enough to make such knaveries yours.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: 'Tis not unknown to you, madam, I am a poor fellow.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Well, sir.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: No, madam, 'tis not so well that I am poor, though many of the rich are damned: but, if I may have your ladyship's good will to go to the world, Isbel the woman and I will do as we may.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Wilt thou needs be a beggar?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I do beg your good will in this case.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: In what case?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: In Isbel's case and mine own. Service is no heritage: and I think I shall never have the blessing of God till I have issue o' my body; for they say barnes are blessings.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Tell me thy reason why thou wilt marry.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: My poor body, madam, requires it: I am driven on by the flesh; and he must needs go that the devil drives.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Is this all your worship's reason?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Faith, madam, I have other holy reasons, such as they are.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: May the world know them?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I have been, madam, a wicked creature, as you and all flesh and blood are; and, indeed, I do marry that I may repent.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Thy marriage, sooner than thy wickedness.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I am out o' friends, madam; and I hope to have friends for my wife's sake.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Such friends are thine enemies, knave.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: You're shallow, madam, in great friends; for the knaves come to do that for me which I am aweary of. He that ears my land spares my team and gives me leave to in the crop; if I be his cuckold, he's my drudge: he that comforts my wife is the cherisher of my flesh and blood; he that cherisheth my flesh and blood loves my flesh and blood is my friend: ergo, blood; he that loves my flesh and blood is he that kisses my wife is my friend. If men could be contented to be what they are, there were no fear in marriage; for young Charbon the Puritan and old Poysam the papist, howsome'er their hearts are severed in religion, their heads are both one; they may joul horns together, like any deer i' the herd.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Wilt thou ever be a foul-mouthed and calumnious knave?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: A prophet I, madam; and I speak the the truth the next way: For I the ballad will repeat, Which men full true shall find; Your marriage comes by dest'ny, Your cuckoo sings by kind.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Get you gone, sir; I'll talk with you more anon.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: May it please you, madam, that he bid Helen come to you: of her I am to speak.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sirrah, tell my gentlewoman I would speak with her; Helen, I mean.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Was this fair face the cause, quoth she, Why the Grecians sacked Troy? Fond done, done fond, Was this King Priam's joy? With that she sighed as she stood, With that she sighed as she stood, And gave this sentence then; Among nine bad if one be good, Among nine bad if one be good, There's yet one good in ten.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: What, one good in ten? you corrupt the song, sirrah.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: One good woman in ten, madam; which is a purifying o' the song: would God would serve the world so all the year; we'ld find no fault with the tithe-woman, if I were the parson. One in ten, quoth a'! An we might have a good woman born but one every blazing star, or at an earthquake, 'twould mend the lottery well: a man may draw his heart out, ere a' pluck one.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: You'll be gone, sir knave, and do as I command you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: That man should be at woman's command, and yet no hurt done! Though honesty be no puritan, yet it will do no hurt; it will wear the surplice of humility over the black gown of a big heart. I am going, forsooth: the business is for Helen to come hither. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Well, now.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: I know, madam, you love your gentlewoman entirely.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Faith, I do: her father bequeathed her to me; and she herself, without other advantage, may lawfully make title to as much love as she finds: there is more owing her than is paid; and more shall be paid her than she'll demand.

sp.speaker: Stew.
sp.p: Madam, I was very late more near her than I think she wished me: alone she was, and did communicate to herself her own words to her own ears; she thought, I dare vow for her, they touched not any stranger sense. Her matter was, she loved your son: Fortune, she said, was no goddess, that had put such difference betwixt their two estates; Love no god, that would not extend his might, only where qualities were level; Dian no queen of virgins, that would suffer her poor knight surprised, without rescue in the first assault or ransom afterward. This she delivered in the most bitter touch of sorrow that e'er I heard virgin exclaim in: which I held my duty speedily to acquaint you withal; sithence, in the loss that may happen, it concerns you something to know it.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
You have discharged this honestly; keep it to yourself: many likelihoods informed me of this before, which hung so tottering in the balance that I could neither believe nor misdoubt. Pray you, leave me: stall this in your bosom; and I thank you for your honest care: I will speak with you further anon. [Exit Steward.
Enter HELENA. Even so it was with me when I was young: If ever we are nature's, these are ours; this thorn Doth to our rose of youth rightly belong; Our blood to us, this to our blood is born; It is the show and seal of nature's truth, Where love's strong passion is impress'd in youth: By our remembrances of days foregone, Such were our faults, or then we thought them
none. Her eye is sick on 't: I observe her now.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What is your pleasure, madam?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: You know, Helen, I am a mother to you.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Mine honourable mistress.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Nay, a mother: Why not a mother? When I said 'a mother,' Methought you saw a serpent: what's in 'mother,' That you start at it? I say, I am your mother; And put you in the catalogue of those That were enwombed mine: 'tis often seen Adoption strives with nature and choice breeds A native slip to us from foreign seeds: You ne'er oppress'd me with a mother's groan, Yet I express to you a mother's care: God's mercy, maiden! does it curd thy blood To say I am thy mother? What's the matter, That this distemper'd messenger of wet The many-colour'd Iris, rounds thine eyes? Why? that you are my daughter?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: That I am not.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I say, I am your mother.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Pardon, madam; The Count Rousillon cannot be my brother: I am from humble, he from honour'd name; No note upon my parents, his all noble: My master, my dear lord he is; and I His servant live, and will his vassal die: He must not be my brother.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Nor I your mother?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
You are my mother, madam; would you
were,-- So that my lord your son were not my brother,-- Indeed my mother or were you both our mothers, I care no more for than I do for heaven, So I were not his sister. Can't no other, But, I your daughter, he must be my brother?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Yes, Helen, you might be my
daughter-in-law: God shield you mean it not! daughter and mother So strive upon your pulse. What, pale again? My fear hath catch'd your fondness: now I see The mystery of your loneliness, and find Your salt tears' head: now to all sense 'tis gross You love my son; invention is ashamed, Against the proclamation of thy passion, To say thou dost not: therefore tell me true; But, tell me then, 'tis so; for, look, thy cheeks Confess it, th' one to th' other; and thine eyes See it so grossly shown in thy behaviours That in their kind they speak it: only sin And hellish obstinacy tie thy tongue, That truth should be suspected. Speak, is 't so? If it be so, you have wound a goodly clew; If it be not, forswear 't: howe'er, I charge thee, As heaven shall work in me for thine avail, Tell me truly.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Good madam, pardon me!

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Do you love my son?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Your pardon, noble mistress!

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Love you my son?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Do not you love him, madam?

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Go not about; my love hath in't a bond, Whereof the world takes note: come, come,
disclose The state of your affection; for your passions Have to the full appeach'd.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Then, I confess, Here on my knee, before high heaven and you, That before you, and next unto high heaven, I love your son. My friends were poor, but honest; so's my love: Be not offended; for it hurts not him That he is loved of me: I follow him not By any token of presumptuous suit; Nor would I have him till I do deserve him; Yet never know how that desert should be. I know I love in vain, strive against hope; Yet in this captious and intenible sieve I still pour in the waters of my love And lack not to lose still: thus, Indian-like, Religious in mine error, I adore The sun, that looks upon his worshipper, But knows of him no more. My dearest madam, Let not your hate encounter with my love For loving where you do: but if yourself, Whose aged honour cites a virtuous youth, Did ever in so true a flame of liking Wish chastely and love dearly, that your Dian Was both herself and love; O, then, give pity To her, whose state is such that cannot choose But lend and give where she is sure to lose; That seeks not to find that her search implies, But riddle-like lives sweetly where she dies!

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Had you not lately an intent, -- speak
truly, -- To go to Paris?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Madam, I had.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Wherefore? tell true.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I will tell truth; by grace itself I swear. You know my father left me some prescriptions Of rare and proved effects, such as his reading And manifest experience had collected For general sovereignty; and that he will'd me In heedfull'st reservation to bestow them, As notes whose faculties inclusive were More than they were in note: amongst the rest There is a remedy, approved, set down, To cure the desperate languishings whereof The king is render'd lost.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: This was your motive For Paris, was it? speak.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: My lord your son made me to think of this; Else Paris and the medicine and the king Had from the conversation of my thoughts Haply been absent then.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: But think you, Helen, If you should tender your supposed aid, He would receive it? he and his physicians Are of a mind; he, that they cannot help him, They, that they cannot help: how shall they credit A poor unlearned virgin, when the schools, Embowell'd of their doctrine, have left off The danger to itself?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
There's something in't, More than my father's skill, which was the greatest Of his profession, that his good receipt Shall for my legacy be sanctified By the luckiest stars in heaven: and, would your
honour But give me leave to try success, I'ld venture The well-lost life of mine on his grace's cure By such a day and hour.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Dost thou believe it?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Ay, madam, knowingly.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Why, Helen, thou shalt have my leave
and love, Means and attendants and my loving greetings To those of mine in court: I'll stay at home And pray God's blessing into thy attempt: Be gone to-morrow; and be sure of this, What I can help thee to thou shalt not miss.
[Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter the KING, attended
with divers young Lords taking leave for the
Florentine war; BERTRAM, and PAROLLES.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Farewell, young lords; these warlike
principles Do not throw from you: and you, my lords,
farewell: Share the advice betwixt you; if both gain, all The gift doth stretch itself as 'tis received, And is enough for both.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: 'Tis our hope, sir, After well enter'd soldiers, to return And find your grace in health.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
No, no, it cannot be; and yet my heart Will not confess he owes the malady That doth my life besiege. Farewell, young
lords; Whether I live or die, be you the sons Of worthy Frenchmen: let higher Italy,-- Those bated that inherit but the fall Of the last monarchy,--see that you come Not to woo honour, but to wed it: when The bravest questant shrinks, find what you seek, That fame may cry you loud: I say, farewell.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p:
Health, at your bidding, serve your
majesty!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Those girls of Italy, take heed of
them: They say, our French lack language to deny, If they demand: beware of being captives, Before you serve.

sp.speaker: Both.
sp.p: Our hearts receive your warnings.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Farewell. Come hither to me.
[Exit, attended.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p:
O my sweet lord, that you will
stay behind us!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: 'Tis not his fault, the spark.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p: O, 'tis brave wars!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Most admirable: I have seen those wars.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
I am commanded here, and kept a coil
with 'Too young' and 'the next year' and 'tis too
early.'

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
An thy mind stand to't boy, steal away
bravely.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
I shall stay here the forehorse to a smock, Creaking my shoes on the plain masonry, Till honour be bought up and no sword worn But one to dance with! By heaven, I'll steal
away.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: There's honour in the theft.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Commit it, count.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p:
I am your accessary; and so,
farewell.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I grow to you, and our parting is a tortured body.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: Farewell, captain.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p: Sweet Monsieur Parolles!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Noble heroes, my sword and yours are kin. Good sparks and lustrous, a word, good metals: you shall find in the regiment of the Spinii one Captain Spurio, with his cicatrice, an emblem of war, here on his sinister cheek; it was this very sword entrenched it: say to him, I live; and observe his reports for me.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p:
We shall, noble captain.
[Exeunt Lords.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Mars dote on you for his novices! what will ye do?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
Stay: the king.
Re-enter KING. BERTRAM and PAROLLES retire.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Use a more spacious ceremony to the noble lords; you have restrained yourself within the list of too cold an adieu: be more expressive to them: for they wear themselves in the cap of the time, there do muster true gait, eat, speak, and move under the influence of the most received star; and though the devil lead the measure, such are to be followed: after them, and take a more dilated farewell.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And I will do so.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
Worthy fellows; and like to prove most sinewy sword-men.
[Exeunt Bertram and Parolles.
Enter LAFEU.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
Pardon, my lord, for me and
for my tidings.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: I'll fee thee to stand up.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
Then here's a man stands, that has
brought his pardon. I would you had kneel'd, my lord, to ask me
mercy, And that at my bidding you could so stand up.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
I would I had; so I had broke thy
pate, And ask'd thee mercy for't.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
Good faith, across: but, my good lord,
'tis thus; Will you be cured of your infirmity?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
O, will you eat no grapes, my royal
fox? Yes, but you will my noble grapes, an if My royal fox could reach them: I have seen a
medicine That's able to breathe life into a stone, Quicken a rock, and make you dance canary With spritely fire and motion; whose simple
touch Is powerful to araise King Pepin, nay, To give great Charlemain a pen in's hand And write to her a love-line.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: What 'her' is this?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
Why, Doctor She: my lord, there's one
arrived, If you will see her: now, by my faith and honour, If seriously I may convey my thoughts In this my light deliverance, I have spoke With one that, in her sex, her years, profession, Wisdom and constancy, hath amazed me more That I dare blame my weakness: will you see
her, For that is her demand, and know her business? That done, laugh well at me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Now, good Lafeu, Bring in the admiration; that we with thee May spend our wonder too, or take off thine By wondering how thou took'st it.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Nay, I'll fit you, And not be all day neither. [Exit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Thus he his special nothing ever
prologues.
Re-enter LAFEU, with HELENA.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Nay, come your ways.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: This haste hath wings indeed.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Nay, come your ways; This is his majesty; say your mind to him: A traitor you do look like; but such traitors His majesty seldom fears: I am Cressid's uncle, That dare leave two together; fare you well. [Exit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Now, fair one, does your business
follow us?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Ay, my good lord. Gerard de Narbon was my father; In what he did profess, well found.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: I knew him.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
The rather will I spare my praises
towards him; Knowing him is enough. On's bed of death Many receipts he gave me; chiefly one, Which, as the dearest issue of his practice, And of his old experience the only darling, He bade me store up, as a triple eye, Safer than mine own two, more dear; I have so; And, hearing your high majesty is touch'd With that malignant cause wherein the honour Of my dear father's gift stands chief in power, I come to tender it and my appliance With all bound humbleness.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: We thank you, maiden; But may not be so credulous of cure, When our most learned doctors leave us and The congregated college have concluded That labouring art can never ransom nature From her inaidible estate; I say we must not So stain our judgement, or corrupt our hope, To prostitute our past-cure malady To empirics, or to dissever so Our great self and our credit, to esteem A senseless help which help past sense we deem.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: My duty then shall pay me for my pains: I will no more enforce mine office on you; Humbly entreating from your royal thoughts A modest one, to bear me back again.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
I cannot give thee less, to be call'd
grateful: Thou thought'st to help me; and such thanks
I give As one near death to those that wish him live: But what at full I know, thou know'st no part, I knowing all my peril, thou no art.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
What I can do can do no hurt to try, Since you set up your rest 'gainst remedy. He that of greatest works is finisher Oft does them by the weakest minister: So holy writ in babes hath judgement shown, When judges have been babes; great floods have
flown From simple sources, and great seas have dried When miracles have by the greatest been denied. Oft expectation fails and most oft there Where most it promises, and oft it hits Where hope is coldest and despair most fits.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
I must not hear thee; fare thee well,
kind maid; Thy pains not used must by thyself be paid: Proffers not took reap thanks for their reward.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Inspired merit so by breath is barr'd: It is not so with Him that all things knows As 'tis with us that square our guess by shows; But most it is presumption in us when The help of heaven we count the act of men. Dear sir, to my endeavours give consent; Of heaven, not me, make an experiment. I am not an impostor that proclaim Myself against the level of mine aim; But know I think and think I know most sure My art is not past power nor you past cure.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Art thou so confident? within what
space Hopest thou my cure?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: The great'st grace lending grace, Ere twice the horses of the sun shall bring Their fiery torcher his diurnal ring, Ere twice in murk and occidental damp Moist Hesperus hath quench'd his sleepy lamp, Or four and twenty times the pilot's glass Hath told the thievish minutes how they pass. What is infirm from your sound parts shall fly, Health shall live free and sickness freely die.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Upon thy certainty and confidence What darest thou venture?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Tax of impudence, A strumpet's boldness, a divulged shame Traduced by odious ballads: my maiden's name Sear'd otherwise; nay, worse--if worse--extended With vilest torture let my life be ended.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Methinks in thee some blessed spirit
doth speak His powerful sound within an organ weak: And what impossibility would slay In common sense, sense saves another way. Thy life 's dear; for all that life can rate Worth name of life in thee hath estimate, Youth, beauty, wisdom, courage, all That happiness and prime can happy call: Thou this to hazard needs and must intimate Skill infinite or monstrous desperate. Sweet practiser, thy physic I will try, That ministers thine own death if I die.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: If I break time, or flinch in property Of what I spoke, unpitied let me die, And well deserved: not helping, death's my fee; But, if help, what do you promise me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Make thy demand.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: But will you make it even?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Ay, by my sceptre and my hopes of
heaven.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
Then shalt thou give me with thy kingly
hand What husband in thy power I will command: Exempted be from me the arrogance To choose from forth the royal blood of France, My low and humble name to propagate With any branch or image of thy state; But such a one, thy vassal, whom I know Is free for me to ask, thee to bestow.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Here is my hand; the premises
observed, Thy will by my performance shall be served: So make the choice of thy own time, for I, Thy resolved patient, on thee still rely. More should I question thee, and more I must, Though more to know could not be more to trust, From whence thou camest, how tended on:
but rest Unquestion'd welcome and undoubted blest. Give me some help here, ho! If thou proceed As high as word, my deed shall match thy meed.
[Flourish. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Come on, sir; I shall now put you to the height of your breeding.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I will show myself highly fed and lowly taught: I know my business is but to the court.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: To the court! why, what place make you special, when you put off that with such contempt? But to the court!

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Truly, madam, if God have lent a man any manners, he may easily put it off at court: he that cannot make a leg, put off's cap, kiss his hand and say nothing, has neither leg, hands, lip, nor cap; and indeed such a fellow, to say precisely, were not for the court; but for me, I have an answer will serve all men.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Marry, that's a bountiful answer that fits all questions.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: It is like a barber's chair that fits all buttocks, the pin-buttock, the quatch-buttock, the brawn buttock, or any buttock.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Will your answer serve fit to all questions?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: As fit as ten groats is for the hand of an attorney, as your French crown for your taffeta punk, as Tib's rush for Tom's forefinger, as a pancake for Shrove Tuesday, a morris for May-day, as the nail to his hole, the cuckold to his horn, as a scolding quean to a wrangling knave, as the nun's lip to the friar's mouth, nay, as the pudding to his skin.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Have you, I say, an answer of such fitness for all questions?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: From below your duke to beneath your constable, it will fit any question.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: It must be an answer of most monstrous size that must fit all demands.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: But a trifle neither, in good faith, if the learned should speak truth of it: here it is, and all that belongs to 't. Ask me if I am a courtier: it shall do you no harm to learn.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: To be young again, if we could: I will be a fool in question, hoping to be the wiser by your answer. I pray you, sir, are you a courtier?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord, sir! There's a simple putting off. More, more, a hundred of them.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Sir, I am a poor friend of yours, that loves you.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord, sir! Thick, thick, spare not me.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: I think, sir, you can eat none of this homely meat.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord, sir! Nay, put me to't, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: You were lately whipped, sir, as I think.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord, sir! spare not me.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Do not cry, 'O Lord, sir!' at your whipping, and 'spare not me'? Indeed your 'O Lord, sir! ' is very sequent to your whipping: you would answer very well to a whipping, if you were but bound to't.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I ne'er had worse luck in my life in my 'O Lord, sir!' I see things may serve long, but not serve ever.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
I play the noble housewife with the
time, To entertain 't so merrily with a fool.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O Lord, sir! why, there't serves well again.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
An end, sir; to your business. Give
Helen this, And urge her to a present answer back: Commend me to my kinsmen and my son: This is not much.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Not much commendation to them.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Not much employment for you: you understand me?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Most fruitfully: I am there before my legs.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Haste you again. [Exeunt severally.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: They say miracles are past; and we have our philosophical persons, to make modern and familiar, things supernatural and causeless. Hence it is that we make trifles of terrors, ensconcing ourselves into seeming knowledge, when we should submit ourselves to an unknown fear.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why, 'tis the rarest argument of wonder that hath shot out in our latter times.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And so 'tis.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: To be relinquished of the artists,--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: So I say.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Both of Galen and Paracelsus.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: So I say.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Of all the learned and authentic fellows,--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Right; so I say.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: That gave him out incurable,--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why, there 'tis; so say I too.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Not to be helped,--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Right: as 'twere, a man assured of a--

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Uncertain life, and sure death.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Just, you say well; so would I have said.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I may truly say, it is a novelty to the world.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: It is, indeed: if you will have it in showing, you shall read it in--what do ye call there?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: A showing of a heavenly effect in an earthly actor.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: That's it; I would have said the very same.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Why, your dolphin is not lustier: 'fore me, I speak in respect--

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Nay, 'tis strange, 'tis very strange, that is the brief and the tedious of it; and he's of a most facinerious spirit that will not acknowledge it to be the--

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Very hand of heaven.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Ay, so I say.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: In a most weak--[pausing]and debile minister, great power, great transcendence: which should, indeed, give us a further use to be made than alone the recovery of the king, as to be-- [pausing]generally thankful.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
I would have said it; you say well. Here comes the king.
Enter KING, HELENA, and Attendants.
LAFEU and PAROLLES retire.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Lustig, as the Dutchman says: I'll like a maid the better, whilst I have a tooth in my head: why, he's able to lead her a coranto.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Mort du vinaigre! is not this Helen?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: 'Fore God, I think so.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Go, call before me all the lords in court. Sit, my preserver, by thy patient's side; And with this healthful hand, whose banish'd sense Thou hast repeal'd, a second time receive The confirmation of my promised gift, Which but attends thy naming.
Enter three or four Lords. Fair maid, send forth thine eye: this youthful
parcel Of noble bachelors stand at my bestowing, O'er whom both sovereign power and father's
voice I have to use: thy frank election make; Thou hast power to choose, and they none to
forsake.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
To each of you one fair and virtuous
mistress Fall, when Love please marry, to each, but
one!

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I'ld give bay Curtal and his furniture, My mouth no more were broken than these boys', And writ as little beard.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Peruse them well: Not one of those but had a noble father.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
Gentlemen, Heaven hath through me restored the king to
health.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p:
We understand it, and thank heaven for
you.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
I am a simple maid, and therein
wealthiest, That I protest I simply am a maid. Please it your majesty, I have done already: The blushes in my cheeks thus whisper me, 'We blush that thou shouldst choose; but, be
refused, Let the white death sit on thy cheek for ever; We'll ne'er come there again.'

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Make choice; and, see Who shuns thy love shuns all his love in me.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Now, Dian, from thy altar do I fly, And to imperial Love, that god most high, Do my sighs stream. Sir, will you hear my suit?

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: And grant it.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
Thanks, sir; all the
rest is mute.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I had rather be in this choice than throw ames-ace for my life.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
The honour, sir, that flames in your fair
eyes, Before I speak, too threateningly replies: Love make your fortunes twenty times above Her that so wishes and her humble love!

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p: No better, if you please.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: My wish receive, Which great Love grant! and so, I take my leave.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Do all they deny her? An they were sons of mine, I'd have them whipped; or I would send them to the Turk to make eunuchs of.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Be not afraid that I your hand should take; I'll never do you wrong for your own sake: Blessing upon your vows! and in your bed Find fairer fortune, if you ever wed!

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: These boys are boys of ice, they'll none have her: sure, they are bastards to the English; the French ne'er got 'em.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
You are too young, too happy, and too
good, To make yourself a son out of my blood.

sp.speaker: Fourth Lord.
sp.p: Fair one, I think not so.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: There's one grape yet; I am sure thy father drunk wine; but if thou be'st not an ass, I am a youth of fourteen; I have known thee already.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
I dare not say I take you;
but I give Me and my service, ever whilst I live, Into your guiding power. This is the man.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Why, then, young Bertram, take her;
she's thy wife.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
My wife, my liege! I shall beseech your
highness, In such a business give me leave to use The help of mine own eyes.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Know'st thou not, Bertram, What she has done for me?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Yes, my good lord; But never hope to know why I should marry her.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Thou know'st she has raised me from
my sickly bed.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: But follows it, my lord, to bring me down Must answer for your raising? I know her well: She had her breeding at my father's charge. A poor physician's daughter my wife! Disdain Rather corrupt me ever!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
'Tis only title thou disdain'st in her,
the which I can build up. Strange is it that our bloods, Of colour, weight, and heat, pour'd all together, Would quite confound distinction, yet stand off In differences so mighty. If she be All that is virtuous, save what thou dislikest, A poor physician's daughter, thou dislikest Of virtue for the name: but do not so: From lowest place when virtuous things proceed, The place is dignified by the doer's deed: Where great additions swell's, and virtue none, It is a dropsied honour. Good alone Is good without a name. Vileness is so: The property by what it is should go, Not by the title. She is young, wise, fair; In these to nature she's immediate heir, And these breed honour: that is honour's scorn, Which challenges itself as honour's born And is not like the sire: honours thrive, When rather from our acts we them derive Than our foregoers: the mere word's a slave Debosh'd on every tomb; on every grave A lying trophy, and as oft is dumb Where dust and damn'd oblivion is the tomb Of honour'd bones indeed. What should be said? If thou canst like this creature as a maid, I can create the rest: virtue and she Is her own dower; honour and wealth from me.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I cannot love her, nor will strive to do't.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Thou wrong'st thyself, if thou shouldst
strive to choose.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
That you are well restored, my lord,
I'm glad: Let the rest go.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
My honour's at the stake; which to
defeat, I must produce my power. Here, take her hand, Proud, scornful boy, unworthy this good gift; Thou dost in vile misprision shackle up My love and her desert; that canst not dream, We, poising us in her defective scale, Shall weigh thee to the beam; that wilt not know, It is in us to plant thine honour where We please to have it grow. Check thy
contempt: Obey our will, which travails in thy good: Believe not thy disdain, but presently Do thine own fortunes that obedient right Which both thy duty owes and our power claims; Or I will throw thee from my care for ever Into the staggers and the careless lapse Of youth and ignorance; both my revenge and
hate Loosing upon thee, in the name of justice, Without all terms of pity. Speak; thine answer.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Pardon, my gracious lord; for I submit My fancy to your eyes: when I consider What great creation and what dole of honour Flies where you bid it, I find that she, which late Was in my nobler thoughts most base, is now The praised of the king; who, so ennobled, Is as 'twere born so.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Take her by the hand, And tell her she is thine; to whom I promise A counterpoise, if not to thy estate A balance more replete.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I take her hand.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
Good fortune and the favour of the king Smile upon this contract; whose ceremony Shall seem expedient on the now-born brief, And be perform'd to-night: the solemn feast Shall more attend upon the coming space, Expecting absent friends. As thou lovest her, Thy love's to me religious; else, does err.
[Exeunt all but Lafeu and Parolles.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Do you hear, monsieur? a word with you.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Your pleasure, sir?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Your lord and master did well to make his recantation.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Recantation! My lord! my master!

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Ay; is it not a language I speak?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: A most harsh one, and not to be understood without bloody succeeding. My master!

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Are you companion to the Count Rousillon?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: To any count, to all counts, to what is man.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: To what is count's man: count's master is of another style.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: You are too old, sir; let it satisfy you, you are too old.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I must tell thee, sirrah, I write man; to which title age cannot bring thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What I dare too well do, I dare not do.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I did think thee, for two ordinaries, to be a pretty wise fellow; thou didst make tolerable vent of thy travel; it might pass: yet the scarfs and the bannerets about thee did manifoldly dissuade me from believing thee a vessel of too great a burthen. I have now found thee; when I lose thee again, I care not: yet art thou good for nothing but taking up; and that thou'rt scarce worth.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Hadst thou not the privilege of antiquity upon thee,--

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Do not plunge thyself too far in anger, lest thou hasten thy trial; which if--Lord have mercy on thee for a hen! So, my good window of lattice, fare thee well: thy casement I need not open, for I look through thee. Give me thy hand.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My lord, you give me most egregious indignity.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Ay, with all my heart; and thou art worthy of it.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I have not, my lord, deserved it.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Yes, good faith, every dram of it; and I will not bate thee a scruple.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Well, I shall be wiser.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Even as soon as thou canst, for thou hast to pull at a smack o' the contrary. If ever thou be'st bound in thy scarf and beaten, thou shalt find what it is to be proud of thy bondage. I have a desire to hold my acquaintance with thee, or rather my knowledge, that I may say in the default, he is a man I know.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: My lord, you do me most insupportable vexation.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: I would it were hell-pains for thy sake, and my poor doing eternal: for doing I am past; as I will by thee, in what motion age will give me leave. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
Well, thou hast a son shall take this disgrace off me; scurvy, old, filthy, scurvy lord! Well, I must be patient; there is no fettering of authority. I'll beat him, by my life, if I can meet him with any convenience, an he were double and double a lord. I'll have no more pity of his age than I would of-- I'll beat him, an if I could but meet him again.
Re-enter LAFEU.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Sirrah, your lord and master's married; there's news for you: you have a new mistress.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I most unfeignedly beseech your lordship to make some reservation of your wrongs: he is my good lord: whom I serve above is my master.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Who? God?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Ay, sir.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: The devil it is that's thy master. Why dost thou garter up thy arms o' this fashion? dost make hose of thy sleeves? do other servants so? Thou wert best set thy lower part where thy nose stands. By mine honor, if I were but two hours younger, I'ld beat thee: methinks, thou art a general offence, and every man should beat thee: I think thou wast created for men to breathe themselves upon thee.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: This is hard and undeserved measure, my lord.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Go to, sir; you were beaten in Italy for picking a kernel out of a pomegranate: you are a vagabond and no true traveller: you you are more saucy with lords and honourable personages than the commission of your birth and virtue gives you heraldry. You are not worth another word, else I'ld call you knave. I leave you. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Par.
Ber.
sp.p: Undone, and forfeited to cares for ever!

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What's the matter, sweet-heart?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
Although before the solemn priest I have
sworn, I will not bed her.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: What, what, sweet-heart?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: O my Parolles, they have married me! I'll to the Tuscan wars, and never bed her.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: France is a dog-hole, and it no more merits The tread of a man's foot: to the wars!

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: There's letters from my mother: what the import is, I know not yet.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
Ay, that would be known. To the wars,
my boy, to the wars! He wears his honour in a box unseen, That hugs his kicky-wicky here at home, Spending his manly marrow in her arms, Which should sustain the bound and high curvet Of Mars's fiery steed. To other regions France is a stable; we that dwell in't jades; Therefore, to the war!

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: It shall be so: I'll send her to my house, Acquaint my mother with my hate to her, And wherefore I am fled; write to the king That which I durst not speak: his present gift Shall furnish me to those Italian fields, Where noble fellows strike: war is no strife To the dark house and the detested wife.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Will this capriccio hold in thee? art sure?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
Go with me to my chamber and advise
me. I'll send her straight away: to-morrow I'll to the wars, she to her single sorrow.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
Why, these balls bound; there's noise
in it. 'Tis hard: A young man married is a man that's marr'd: Therefore away, and leave her bravely; go: The king has done you wrong: but, hush, 'tis so. [Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: My mother greets me kindly: is she well?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: She is not well; but yet she has her health: she's very merry; but yet she is not well: but thanks be given, she's very well and wants nothing i' the world; but she is not well.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: If she be very well, what does she ail that she's not very well?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Truly, she's very well indeed, but for two things.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What two things?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p:
One, that she's not in heaven, whither God send her quickly! the other, that she's in earth, from whence God send her quickly!
Enter PAROLLES.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Bless you, my fortunate lady!

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I hope, sir, I have your good will to have mine own good fortunes.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: You had my prayers to lead them on; and to keep them on, have them still. O, my knave, how does my old lady?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: So that you had her wrinkles and I her money, I would she did as you say.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why, I say nothing.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Marry, you are the wiser man; for many a man's tongue shakes out his master's undoing: to say nothing, to do nothing, to know nothing, and to have nothing, is to be a great part of your title; which is within a very little of nothing.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Away! thou'rt a knave.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: You should have said, sir, before a knave thou'rt a knave; that's, before me thou'rt a knave: this had been truth, sir.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Go to, thou art a witty fool; I have found thee.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Did you find me in yourself, sir? or were you taught to find me? The search, sir, was profitable; and much fool may you find in you, even to the world's pleasure and the increase of laughter.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
A good knave, i' faith, and well fed. Madam, my lord will go away to-night; A very serious business calls on him. The great prerogative and rite of love, Which, as your due, time claims, he does
acknowledge; But puts it off to a compell'd restraint; Whose want, and whose delay, is strew'd with
sweets, Which they distil now in the curbed time, To make the coming hour o'erflow with joy And pleasure drown the brim.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What's his will else?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p:
That you will take your instant leave o'
the king, And make this haste as your own good
proceeding, Strengthen'd with what apology you think May make it probable need.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: What more commands he?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: That, having this obtain'd, you presently Attend his further pleasure.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: In every thing I wait upon his will.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I shall report it so.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I pray you. [Exit Parolles. Come, sirrah. [Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: But I hope your lordship thinks not him a soldier.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Yes, my lord, and of very valiant approof.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You have it from his own deliverance.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: And by other warranted testimony.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Then my dial goes not true: I took this lark for a bunting.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I do assure you, my lord, he is very great in knowledge and accordingly valiant.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p:
I have then sinned against his experience and transgressed against his valour; and my state that way is dangerous, since I cannot yet find in my heart to repent. Here he comes: I pray you, make us friends; I will pursue the amity.
Enter PAROLLES.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: These things shall be done, sir.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: Pray you, sir, who's his tailor?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Sir?

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: O, I know him well, I, sir; he, sir, 's a good workman, a very good tailor.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Is she gone to the king?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: She is.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Will she away to-night?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: As you'll have her.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
I have writ my letters, casketed my
treasure, Given order for our horses; and to-night, When I should take possession of the bride, End ere I do begin.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: A good traveller is something at the latter end of a dinner; but one that lies three thirds and uses a known truth to pass a thousand nothings with, should be once heard and thrice beaten. God save you, captain.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Is there any unkindness between my lord and you, monsieur?

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: I know not how I have deserved to run into my lord's displeasure.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: You have made shift to run into't, boots and spurs and all, like him that leaped into the custard; and out of it you'll run again, rather than suffer question for your residence.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: It may be you have mistaken him, my lord.

sp.speaker: Laf.
sp.p: And shall do so ever, though I took him at's prayers. Fare you well, my lord; and believe this of me, there can be no kernel in this light nut; the soul of this man is his clothes. Trust him not in matter of heavy consequence; I have kept of them tame, and know their natures. Farewell, monsieur: I have spoken better of you than you have or will to deserve at my hand; but we must do good against evil. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: An idle lord, I swear.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Why, do you not know him?

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
Yes, I do know him well, and common
speech Gives him a worthy pass. Here comes my clog.
Enter HELENA.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I have, sir, as I was commanded from you, Spoke with the king and have procured his leave For present parting; only he desires Some private speech with you.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
I shall obey his will. You must not marvel, Helen, at my course, Which holds not colour with the time, nor does The ministration and required office On my particular. Prepared I was not For such a business; therefore am I found So much unsettled: this drives me to entreat you That presently you take your way for home; And rather muse than ask why I entreat you, For my respects are better than they seem And my appointments have in them a need Greater than shows itself at the first view To you that know them not. This to my mother:
[Giving a letter. 'Twill be two days ere I shall see you, so I leave you to your wisdom.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Sir, I can nothing say, But that I am your most obedient servant.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Come, come, no more of that.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: And ever shall With true observance seek to eke out that Wherein toward me my homely stars have fail'd To equal my great fortune.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Let that go: My haste is very great: farewell; hie home.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Pray, sir, your pardon.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Well, what would you say?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: I am not worthy of the wealth I owe, Nor dare I say 'tis mine, and yet it is; But, like a timorous thief, most fain would steal What law does vouch mine own.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: What would you have?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
Something; and scarce so much: nothing,
indeed. I would not tell you what I would, my lord: Faith, yes; Strangers and foes do sunder, and not kiss.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
I pray you, stay not, but in haste to
horse.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
I shall not break your bidding, good my
lord.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p:
Where are my other men, monsieur?
Farewell. [Exit Helena. Go thou toward home; where I will never come Whilst I can shake my sword or hear the drum. Away, and for our flight.

sp.speaker: Par.
sp.p: Bravely, coragio! [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter the DUKE of Florence, attended;
the two Frenchmen, with a troop of soldiers.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
So that from point to point now have
you heard The fundamental reasons of this war, Whose great decision hath much blood let forth And more thirsts after.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p: Holy seems the quarrel Upon your grace's part; black and fearful On the opposer.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
Therefore we marvel much our cousin
France Would in so just a business shut his bosom Against our borrowing prayers.

sp.speaker: Sec. Lord.
sp.p: Good, my lord, The reasons of our state I cannot yield, But like a common and an outward man, That the great figure of a council frames By self-unable motion: therefore dare not Say what I think of it, since I have found Myself in my incertain grounds to fail As often as I guess'd.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Be it his pleasure.

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.p:
But I am sure the younger of our
nature, That surfeit on their ease, will day by day Come here for physic.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Welcome shall they be; And all the honours that can fly from us Shall on them settle. You know your places well; When better fall, for your avails they fell: To-morrow to the field. [Flourish. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: It hath happened all as I would have had it, save that he comes not along with her.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: By my troth, I take my young lord to be a very melancholy man.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: By what observance, I pray you?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Why, he will look upon his boot and sing; mend the ruff and sing; ask questions and sing; pick his teeth and sing. I know a man that had this trick of melancholy sold a goodly manor for a song.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Let me see what he writes, and when he means to come. [Opening a letter.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: I have no mind to Isbel since I was at court: our old ling and our Isbels o' the country are nothing like your old ling and your Isbels o' the court: the brains of my Cupid's knocked out, and I begin to love, as an old man loves money, with no stomach.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: What have we here?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: E'en that you have there. [Exit.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
I have sent you a daughter-in-law: she hath recovered the king, and undone me. I have wedded her, not bedded her; and sworn to make the 'not' eternal. You shall hear I am run away: know it before the report come. If there be breadth enough in the world, I will hold a long distance. My duty to you. Your unfortunate son, BERTRAM. This is not well, rash and unbridled boy, To fly the favours of so good a king; To pluck his indignation on thy head By the misprising of a maid too virtuous For the contempt of empire.
Re-enter CLOWN.

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: O madam, yonder is heavy news within between two soldiers and my young lady!

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p: Nay, there is some comfort in the news, some comfort; your son will not be killed so soon as I thought he would.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Why should he be killed?

sp.speaker: Clo.
sp.p:
So say I, madam, if he run away, as I hear he does: the danger is in standing to 't; that's the loss of men, though it be the getting of children. Here they come will tell you more: for my part, I only hear your son was run away. [Exit.
Enter HELENA and two Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p: Save you, good madam.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Madam, my lord is gone, for ever gone.

sp.speaker: Sec. Gent.
sp.p: Do not say so.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Think upon patience. Pray you,
gentlemen, I have felt so many quirks of joy and grief, That the first face of neither, on the start, Can woman me unto't: where is my son, I pray
you?

sp.speaker: Sec. Gent.
sp.p:
Madam, he's gone to serve the
duke of Florence: We met him thitherward; for thence we came, And, after some dispatch in hand at court, Thither we bend again.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
Look on his letter, madam; here's my
passport. [Reads]When thou canst get the ring upon my finger which never shall come off, and show me a child begotten of thy body that I am father to, then call me husband: but in such a 'then' I write a 'never.' This is a dreadful sentence.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Brought you this letter, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p: Ay, madam; And for the contents' sake are sorry for our pains.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
I prithee, lady, have a better cheer; If thou engrossest all the griefs are thine, Thou robb'st me of a moiety: he was my son; But I do wash his name out of my blood, And thou art all my child. Towards Florence is
he?

sp.speaker: Sec. Gent.
sp.p: Ay, madam.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: And to be a soldier?

sp.speaker: Sec. Gent.
sp.p:
Such is his noble purpose; and,
believe 't, The duke will lay upon him all the honour That good convenience claims.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Return you thither?

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p:
Ay, madam, with the swiftest
wing of speed.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
[Reads.] Till I have no wife I have
nothing in France. 'Tis bitter.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Find you that there?

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p: Ay, madam.

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p: 'Tis but the boldness of his hand, haply, which his heart was not consenting to.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Nothing in France, until he have no
wife! There's nothing here that is too good for him But only she; and she deserves a lord That twenty such rude boys might tend upon And call her hourly mistress. Who was with
him?

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p: A servant only, and a gentleman Which I have some time known.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: Parolles, was it not?

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p: Ay, my good lady, he.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
A very tainted fellow, and full of
wickedness. My son corrupts a well-derived nature With his inducement.

sp.speaker: First Gent.
sp.p: Indeed, good lady, The fellow has a deal of that too much, Which holds him much to have.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: You're welcome, gentlemen. I will entreat you, when you see my son, To tell him that his sword can never win The honour that he loses: more I'll entreat you Written to bear along.

sp.speaker: Sec. Gent.
sp.p: We serve you, madam, In that and all your worthiest affairs.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Not so, but as we change our
courtesies. Will you draw near?
[Exeunt Countess and Gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Hel.
sp.p:
'Till I have no wife, I have nothing in
France.' Nothing in France, until he has no wife! Thou shalt have none, Rousillon, none in France; Then hast thou all again. Poor lord! is 't I That chase thee from thy country and expose Those tender limbs of thine to the event Of the none-sparing war? and is it I That drive thee from the sportive court, where
thou Wast shot at with fair eyes, to be the mark Of smoky muskets? O you leaden messengers, That ride upon the violent speed of fire, Fly with false aim; move the still-peering air, That sings with piercing; do not touch my lord Whoever shoots at him, I set him there; Whoever charges on his forward breast, I am the caitiff that do hold him to't; And, though I kill him not, I am the cause His death was so effected: better 'twere I met the ravin lion when he roar'd With sharp constraint of hunger; better 'twere That all the miseries which nature owes Were mine at once. No, come thou home,
Rousillon, Whence honour but of danger wins a scar, As oft it loses all: I will be gone; My being here it is that holds thee hence: Shall I stay here to do't? no, no, although The air of paradise did fan the house And angels officed all: I will be gone, That pitiful rumour may report my flight, To consolate thine ear. Come, night; end, day! For with the dark, poor thief, I'll steal away. [Exit.

div.head: SCENE III
div.stage:
Enter the DUKE of Florence,
BERTRAM, PAROLLES, Soldiers, Drum, and
Trumpets.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p:
The general of our horse thou art;
and we, Great in our hope, lay our best love and credence Upon thy promising fortune.

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: Sir, it is A charge too heavy for my strength, but yet We'll strive to bear it for your worthy sake To the extreme edge of hazard.

sp.speaker: Duke.
sp.p: Then go thou forth; And fortune play upon thy prosperous helm, As thy auspicious mistress!

sp.speaker: Ber.
sp.p: This very day, Great Mars, I put myself into thy file: Make me but like my thoughts, and I shall prove A lover of thy drum, hater of love. [Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Alas! and would you take the letter
of her? Might you not know she would do as she has done, By sending me a letter? Read it again.

sp.speaker: Steward.
sp.p:
[Reads.] I am Saint Jaques' pilgrim, thither gone: Ambitious love hath so in me offended, That barefoot plod I the cold ground upon, With sainted vow my faults to have amended. Write, write, that from the bloody course of war My dearest master, your dear son, may hie: Bless him at home in peace, whilst I from far His name with zealous fervour sanctify: His taken labours bid him me forgive; I, his despiteful Juno, sent him forth From courtly friends, with camping foes to live, Where death and danger dogs the heels of
worth: He is too good and fair for death and me; Whom I myself embrace, to set him free.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p:
Ah, what sharp stings are in her
mildest words! Rinaldo, you did never lack advice so much, As letting her pass so: had I spoke with her, I could have well diverted her intents, Which thus she hath prevented.

sp.speaker: Steward.
sp.p:
[Reads.]
Pardon me, madam: If I had given you this at over-night, She might have been o'erta'en; and yet she
writes, Pursuit would be but vain.

sp.speaker: Count.
sp.p: What angel shall Bless this unworthy husband? he cannot thrive, Unless her prayers, whom heaven delights to hear And loves to grant, reprieve him from the wrath Of greatest justice. Write, write, Rinaldo, To this unworthy husband of his wife; Let every word weigh heavy of her worth That he does weigh too light: my greatest grief, Though little he do feel it, set down sharply. Dispatch the most convenient messenger: When haply he shall hear that she is gone, He will return; and hope I may that she, Hearing so much, will speed her foot again, Led hither by pure love: which of them both Is dearest to me, I have no skill in sense To make distinction: provide this messenger: My heart is heavy and mine age is weak; Grief would have tears, and sorrow bids me speak. [Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE V
div.stage:
Florence. Without the walls. A
tucket afar off.

Enter an old Widow of Florence, DIANA,
VIOLENTA, and MARIANA, with other Citizens.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: Nay, come; for if they do approach the city, we shall lose all the sight.

sp.speaker: Dia.
sp.p: They say the French count has done most honourable service.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: It is reported that he has taken their greatest commander; and that with his own hand he slew the duke's brother. [Tucket.] We have lost our labour; they are gone a contrary way: hark! you may know by their trumpets.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: Come, let's return again, and suffice ourselves with the report of it. Well, Diana, take heed of this French earl: the honour of a maid is her name; and no legacy is so rich as honesty.

sp.speaker: Wid.
sp.p: I have told my neighbour how you have been solicited by a gentleman his companion.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.p: I know that knave; hang him! one Parolles: a filthy officer he is in those suggestions for the young earl.
